pages.h1: Business owner's policy (BOP) insurance in Florida
pages.title: BOP Insurance in Florida: Business Owner's Policy | AlphaGen
pages.description: What a BOP bundles for a small Florida business, who qualifies, and what insurers ask for before they quote one.
pages.card_text: Property and liability packaged together for smaller businesses.
pages.intro: A business owner's policy packages commercial property and general liability into one policy for smaller businesses that fit an insurer's eligibility rules. It is often the simplest starting point for an office, a shop or a service business.
who: Small and mid-sized businesses with a modest building or contents value and a lower-hazard operation: offices, retail shops, many service businesses, some restaurants and some contractors.
Insurers set eligibility by class of business, revenue, square footage and building size, so a business that outgrows those limits usually moves to separate property and liability policies.
includes: Property — the building if you own it, and your business personal property (furniture, equipment, inventory).
General liability — third-party bodily injury and property damage arising from your premises and operations.
Business income — lost income while you cannot operate after a covered property loss, on many forms.
Optional endorsements — such as equipment breakdown, cyber, hired and non-owned auto, or employment practices, depending on the insurer.

faqs.q: Is a BOP the same as general liability insurance?
faqs.a: No. A BOP includes general liability, but it also includes property insurance for the building and contents, so it is broader than a general liability policy on its own.
faqs.a_plain: No. A BOP includes general liability, but it also includes property insurance for the building and contents, so it is broader than a general liability policy on its own.

faqs.q: Does a BOP include workers' compensation?
faqs.a: No. Workers' compensation is always a separate policy. A BOP does not insure injuries to your own employees.
faqs.a_plain: No. Workers' compensation is always a separate policy. A BOP does not insure injuries to your own employees.

faqs.q: Does a BOP include flood?
faqs.a: Usually not. Flood is commonly excluded from commercial property forms, including BOPs, and is placed on a separate flood policy.
faqs.a_plain: Usually not. Flood is commonly excluded from commercial property forms, including BOPs, and is placed on a separate flood policy.

pages.title: General Liability Insurance in Florida | AlphaGen
pages.description: What commercial general liability is built for, who needs it in Florida, and what an underwriter asks for to quote it.
pages.card_text: Third-party injury and property-damage claims against your business.
pages.intro: Commercial general liability (CGL) responds to claims that your business caused bodily injury or property damage to someone else, or certain personal and advertising injury. It is the policy landlords, clients and general contractors most often ask to see a certificate for.
who: Almost every business that deals with the public, works at a customer's site, or signs a contract or lease that requires proof of insurance.
Contractors, retailers, restaurants, property owners and service businesses are the most frequent buyers; the class of business shapes the price more than anything else.
includes: Premises and operations — injuries or damage at your location or caused by your work.
Products and completed operations — claims arising from what you sold or work you finished.
Personal and advertising injury — such as certain defamation or copyright claims in your advertising.
Defense costs — most forms fund the defense of a covered claim; whether that reduces your limit depends on the form.

faqs.q: Is general liability required in Florida?

faqs.q: Does general liability cover my employees' injuries?

pages.title: Workers' Compensation Insurance in Florida | AlphaGen
pages.description: Who must carry workers' comp in Florida, how premium is built from payroll and class codes, and what insurers ask for.
pages.card_text: Medical care and wage benefits for employees hurt on the job.
pages.intro: Workers' compensation pays medical care and lost-wage benefits to employees injured on the job, under Florida's workers' compensation law, and generally limits employees' right to sue the employer for those injuries. Premium is built from payroll by job classification, not a flat price.
who: Florida employers who meet the state's employee-count thresholds, which are lower for construction businesses than for most other industries. The thresholds and the exemptions are set out in Florida's workers' compensation law, Chapter 440.
Businesses that hire subcontractors, because a contractor can become responsible for an uninsured subcontractor's workers.
includes: Workers' compensation (Part One) — the medical and indemnity benefits Florida law requires.
Employer's liability (Part Two) — certain lawsuits by employees or others arising from a work injury that fall outside the workers' compensation system.
Audit-based premium — the premium is estimated at the start and adjusted after the policy year to actual payroll.

faqs.q: How is workers' comp premium calculated?
faqs.a: Roughly: payroll for each job classification, divided by one hundred, multiplied by that class's rate, then adjusted by your experience modification factor and any credits or surcharges. That is why it is quoted per hundred dollars of payroll rather than as a flat price.
faqs.a_plain: Roughly: payroll for each job classification, divided by one hundred, multiplied by that class's rate, then adjusted by your experience modification factor and any credits or surcharges. That is why it is quoted per hundred dollars of payroll rather than as a flat price.

faqs.q: What is an experience mod?
faqs.a: An experience modification factor compares your past claims with what is expected for businesses of your size and type. A mod below one lowers premium; a mod above one raises it. Insurers ask for your current mod worksheet if you have one.
faqs.a_plain: An experience modification factor compares your past claims with what is expected for businesses of your size and type. A mod below one lowers premium; a mod above one raises it. Insurers ask for your current mod worksheet if you have one.

faqs.q: Why is there an audit at the end of the year?
faqs.a: Because the premium is based on payroll, the insurer checks your actual payroll after the policy year and adjusts the premium up or down.
faqs.a_plain: Because the premium is based on payroll, the insurer checks your actual payroll after the policy year and adjusts the premium up or down.

faqs.q: Does an independent subcontractor need to be covered?
faqs.a: It depends on the facts. Florida law can make a contractor responsible for an uninsured subcontractor's workers, so insurers ask for certificates of insurance from subcontractors.

pages.title: Commercial Property Insurance in Florida | AlphaGen
pages.description: Commercial property insurance for Florida buildings and contents: wind, valuation, deductibles, and what underwriters ask.
pages.card_text: Buildings, equipment and inventory, including Florida wind questions.
pages.intro: Commercial property insurance responds to physical loss or damage to the buildings you own and the property your business uses, subject to the causes of loss the policy lists and the ones it excludes. In Florida, how wind and hurricane are handled is usually the biggest question.
who: Business owners who own their building, landlords of commercial space, and tenants who need to insure improvements, equipment and inventory.
Lenders usually require it on a financed building, with the lender named on the policy.
includes: Building — the structure, if you own it or your lease makes you responsible for it.
Business personal property — furniture, fixtures, equipment and stock.
Business income and extra expense — on many forms, lost income and extra costs after a covered loss.
Wind and hurricane — included, written with a separate deductible, or excluded and placed elsewhere, depending on the insurer and the location.

faqs.q: What is a named-storm or hurricane deductible?
faqs.a: A separate deductible that applies to wind damage from a named storm or hurricane. In Florida it is often a percentage of the insured value rather than a flat dollar amount, so read it before renewal.
faqs.a_plain: A separate deductible that applies to wind damage from a named storm or hurricane. In Florida it is often a percentage of the insured value rather than a flat dollar amount, so read it before renewal.

faqs.q: Replacement cost or actual cash value?
faqs.a: Replacement cost pays to repair or replace without deducting for depreciation; actual cash value deducts it. The choice changes both the premium and what a claim pays.
faqs.a_plain: Replacement cost pays to repair or replace without deducting for depreciation; actual cash value deducts it. The choice changes both the premium and what a claim pays.

pages.intro: A rental property needs a landlord policy, not a homeowners policy. Single-family rentals and condos are usually written on a dwelling fire form; small apartment buildings on a commercial habitational policy. Both answer different questions from the policy on the home you live in.

pages.description: Cyber insurance for Florida small businesses: breach response, liability and the security controls insurers now ask about.
pages.card_text: Breach response, ransomware and data-privacy liability.
pages.intro: Cyber insurance responds to data breaches, ransomware and other network events, both the costs of responding and claims from people whose data was exposed. Insurers now price it largely on the security controls you already have in place.
who: Any business that holds customer, patient or employee data, takes card payments, or depends on email and computers to operate.
Florida businesses subject to the state's data-breach notification law, Fla. Stat. section 501.171.
includes: First-party response costs — forensics, notification, credit monitoring and legal advice after a breach.
Business interruption — income lost while systems are down, on many forms.
Cyber extortion — ransomware response, subject to the policy's terms.
Third-party liability — claims and some regulatory proceedings arising from a breach.

Businesses asked for a license or permit bond by a state agency or a local government.
includes: Bid bonds — that you will sign the contract and provide the final bonds if your bid is accepted.
Performance bonds — that you will complete the contract according to its terms.
Payment bonds — that your subcontractors and suppliers will be paid.
License and permit bonds — that you will follow the laws and rules tied to a license or permit.

faqs.q: Is a surety bond the same as insurance?
faqs.a: No. A bond protects the obligee, not your business. Before issuing a bond, the surety usually has the business, and often its owners, sign an indemnity agreement promising to repay any claim it pays.
faqs.a_plain: No. A bond protects the obligee, not your business. Before issuing a bond, the surety usually has the business, and often its owners, sign an indemnity agreement promising to repay any claim it pays.

faqs.q: What is bonding capacity?
faqs.a: The size of a single contract and the total of all bonded work a surety will support for you. It is set from your financial statements, your experience and the work you already have underway.
faqs.a_plain: The size of a single contract and the total of all bonded work a surety will support for you. It is set from your financial statements, your experience and the work you already have underway.

faqs.q: Why does the surety want my personal financial information?
faqs.a: For most small and mid-sized businesses, the owners personally sign the indemnity agreement, so the surety looks at their finances and credit as well as the company's.
faqs.a_plain: For most small and mid-sized businesses, the owners personally sign the indemnity agreement, so the surety looks at their finances and credit as well as the company's.

faqs.q: How long does it take to get a bond?
faqs.a: Many license and permit bonds can be issued quickly from a short application. Contract bonds take longer, because the surety reviews your financial statements and work in progress first.
faqs.a_plain: Many license and permit bonds can be issued quickly from a short application. Contract bonds take longer, because the surety reviews your financial statements and work in progress first.

faqs.q: What drives the price of a bond?
faqs.a: The type and amount of the bond, the financial strength and credit of the business and its owners, and your experience with similar work.
faqs.a_plain: The type and amount of the bond, the financial strength and credit of the business and its owners, and your experience with similar work.

items.text: The bond type, the bond amount and who requires it (the obligee)
A copy of the bond form, or the contract, license or permit requirement that calls for the bond
Business financial statements, prepared by a certified public accountant for larger bond programs
A work-in-progress schedule: contracts underway, their value and how far along each one is
items.why: it shows how much unfinished work the surety would already be backing

items.text: Your bank line of credit and bank reference
Owners' personal financial statements and consent to a credit check
items.why: owners usually sign the indemnity agreement personally

items.text: Your largest completed projects and the experience of your key people
Any past bond claims, contract defaults or unfinished projects

pages.h1: Employment practices liability insurance (EPLI) in Florida
pages.title: Employment Practices Liability (EPLI) in Florida | AlphaGen
pages.description: EPLI for Florida employers: discrimination, harassment and wrongful-termination claims, claims-made terms and what insurers ask.
pages.card_text: Claims by employees and applicants over how they were treated.
pages.intro: Employment practices liability insurance responds to claims by employees, former employees and job applicants alleging wrongful employment acts, such as discrimination, harassment, wrongful termination and retaliation. General liability policies commonly exclude these claims, and workers' compensation does not address them.
who: Any business with employees. Claims come from hiring, discipline, promotion and termination decisions, not only at large employers.
Businesses with high turnover, recent layoffs, or no dedicated human-resources staff.
Businesses whose employees deal with the public, which may want coverage for harassment claims brought by customers or other third parties.
includes: Employment claims — discrimination, harassment, wrongful termination, retaliation and similar allegations.
Defense costs — on many forms these are paid inside the limit, so they reduce what is left for a settlement.
Third-party coverage — claims by customers or vendors, where the insurer offers it as an option.
Claims-made terms — the policy responds to claims first made while it is in force, subject to a retroactive date.

faqs.q: Isn't this covered by my general liability policy?
faqs.a: Usually not. General liability policies commonly exclude employment-related claims, which is why EPLI is a separate policy or endorsement.
faqs.a_plain: Usually not. General liability policies commonly exclude employment-related claims, which is why EPLI is a separate policy or endorsement.

faqs.q: What does claims-made mean?
faqs.a: The policy responds to claims first made during the policy period, for acts after its retroactive date. Keeping coverage continuous protects that retroactive date when you renew or change insurers.
faqs.a_plain: The policy responds to claims first made during the policy period, for acts after its retroactive date. Keeping coverage continuous protects that retroactive date when you renew or change insurers.

faqs.q: Are wage-and-hour claims covered?
faqs.a: Usually not. Most EPLI policies exclude wage-and-hour claims, though some offer a limited amount for defense. Check the specific policy.
faqs.a_plain: Usually not. Most EPLI policies exclude wage-and-hour claims, though some offer a limited amount for defense. Check the specific policy.

faqs.q: How much does EPLI cost in Florida?
faqs.a: What drives the price is the business itself: the number of employees and where they work, turnover and recent layoffs, your written employment practices, your claims history, and the limits and retention chosen.
faqs.a_plain: What drives the price is the business itself: the number of employees and where they work, turnover and recent layoffs, your written employment practices, your claims history, and the limits and retention chosen.

items.text: Legal name, entity type and FEIN
Years in business and a description of operations
Locations and, where relevant, the class code that best describes the business
items.why: the class code sets which rating base and rate an underwriter uses

items.text: Number of full-time, part-time and seasonal employees and independent contractors, and where they work
Turnover and terminations in the past year, and any layoffs made or planned
items.why: terminations and layoffs are where most employment claims begin

items.text: An employee handbook with anti-harassment, complaint and discipline procedures
Who handles human resources: your own staff, an outside firm or a professional employer organization
Training for managers and staff
Past charges with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission or the state, demand letters and lawsuits, and any known circumstances
Your current EPLI insurer and retroactive date, if any

pages.title: Homeowners Insurance in Florida | AlphaGen
pages.description: Florida homeowners insurance explained: wind and hurricane deductibles, roof and wind-mitigation questions, and what insurers ask.
pages.card_text: Primary homes and high-value homes, including wind questions.
pages.intro: A homeowners policy insures the home you live in, your belongings and your personal liability. In Florida the answers that matter most are about wind: the hurricane deductible, the roof, and the wind-mitigation features the inspector records.
who: Owners of a single-family home they live in, from a starter home to a high-value or coastal property.
Buyers who need proof of coverage before closing, since lenders require it.
includes: Dwelling and other structures — the house, plus detached structures such as a fence or shed.
Personal property — your belongings, with special limits on certain items such as jewelry.
Loss of use — extra living costs while the home cannot be lived in after a covered loss.
Personal liability — claims that you injured someone or damaged their property.

faqs.q: Is flood part of homeowners insurance?
faqs.a: No. Flood is excluded from standard homeowners policies and is written on a separate flood policy.
faqs.a_plain: No. Flood is excluded from standard homeowners policies and is written on a separate flood policy.

faqs.q: What is a hurricane deductible?
faqs.a: A separate deductible for hurricane wind damage, often a percentage of the dwelling limit. In Florida it generally applies once per calendar season rather than once per storm.
faqs.a_plain: A separate deductible for hurricane wind damage, often a percentage of the dwelling limit. In Florida it generally applies once per calendar season rather than once per storm.

faqs.q: Why does the insurer want a wind-mitigation inspection?
faqs.a: Florida requires insurers to offer premium discounts for features that reduce wind damage, such as roof-to-wall connections and opening protection. The inspection documents those features.
faqs.a_plain: Florida requires insurers to offer premium discounts for features that reduce wind damage, such as roof-to-wall connections and opening protection. The inspection documents those features.

faqs.q: How much does homeowners insurance cost in Florida?
faqs.a: What drives the price is the property itself: its location and flood zone, its age, roof and construction, its wind-mitigation features, the coverage limits and deductibles chosen, and its claims history.
faqs.a_plain: What drives the price is the property itself: its location and flood zone, its age, roof and construction, its wind-mitigation features, the coverage limits and deductibles chosen, and its claims history.

items.text: Year built, construction, square footage and number of stories
Roof type, age and condition, and the year of the last full replacement
items.why: Florida law (Florida Statutes section 627.7011) limits refusing or non-renewing a policy on roof age alone for newer roofs, and an inspection can show remaining life on older roofs

items.text: Updates to wiring, plumbing and heating and cooling
Pools, docks and other features
For high-value homes, a replacement-cost estimate, scheduled jewelry, art or collections, and central-station alarms
A wind-mitigation inspection on Florida's OIR-B1-1802 form
items.why: the features it records earn premium credits Florida requires insurers to offer

items.text: A four-point inspection for older homes, and a roof inspection where asked
items.why: many insurers ask for one on older homes, and some will not quote without it

items.text: Your flood zone and, if you have one, an elevation certificate
Claims in the past five years, your current insurer and your renewal date

pages.title: Condo Insurance (HO-6) in Florida | AlphaGen
pages.description: What a Florida condo unit-owner (HO-6) policy is for, how it fits the association's master policy, and what insurers ask.
pages.card_text: Unit-owner coverage that fits around the association's master policy.
pages.intro: A condo unit-owner policy, usually called an HO-6, insures what the association's master policy does not: your belongings, the parts of the unit your declaration makes your responsibility, your liability, and often loss assessments.
who: Owners of a condominium unit they live in, and owners who rent their unit out (who need a policy written for rentals).
Buyers whose lender requires an HO-6 before closing.
includes: Unit improvements and fixtures — the parts of the unit your condo documents make the owner's responsibility.
Personal property — your belongings inside the unit.
Loss assessment — your share of a special assessment after a covered loss, on many forms.
Personal liability and loss of use.

faqs.q: Doesn't the association insure my unit?
faqs.a: Partly. Florida's condominium law divides what the association insures from what the unit owner insures, and your declaration fills in the details. The HO-6 covers your side of that line.
faqs.a_plain: Partly. Florida's condominium law divides what the association insures from what the unit owner insures, and your declaration fills in the details. The HO-6 covers your side of that line.

faqs.q: What documents will the insurer ask for?
faqs.a: Often your declarations page from the master policy or the association's insurance summary, and details of any upgrades you made to the unit.
faqs.a_plain: Often your declarations page from the master policy or the association's insurance summary, and details of any upgrades you made to the unit.

faqs.q: Do I need flood insurance in a condo?
faqs.a: Possibly. The master policy may or may not carry flood, and it will not cover your belongings. Ask for a separate unit-owner flood quote.
faqs.a_plain: Possibly. The master policy may or may not carry flood, and it will not cover your belongings. Ask for a separate unit-owner flood quote.

faqs.q: How much does condo insurance cost in Florida?
faqs.a: What drives the price is the property itself: its location and flood zone, its age, roof and construction, its wind-mitigation features, the coverage limits and deductibles chosen, and its claims history.
faqs.a_plain: What drives the price is the property itself: its location and flood zone, its age, roof and construction, its wind-mitigation features, the coverage limits and deductibles chosen, and its claims history.

items.text: The association's master-policy summary: what it insures inside the unit and its deductibles
items.why: the master policy decides where your unit coverage has to start

items.text: Improvements and upgrades you have made
The floor the unit is on, the building's year built and its updates
The loss-assessment limit you want
Whether you live in the unit or rent it out
A wind-mitigation report for the building, if the association has one
Your flood zone
Claims in the past five years and your current insurer

pages.title: Private Flood Insurance in Florida | AlphaGen
pages.description: Private flood insurance in Florida: how it differs from NFIP flood, what an elevation certificate does, and what insurers ask.
pages.card_text: Flood coverage from private insurers for homes and businesses.
pages.intro: Flood is excluded from homeowners, condo and most commercial property policies. Private flood insurers write it as a separate policy, often with different limits, waiting periods and terms from the federal National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP).
who: Florida homeowners, condo owners and businesses in or near a flood zone, and anyone whose lender requires flood coverage.
Owners who need higher limits or different terms than a federal flood policy offers.
includes: Building — the structure, up to the limit chosen.
Contents — usually a separate limit you choose.
Loss of use or business income — on some private forms.
Replacement cost — available on some private forms; terms vary widely.

faqs.q: Will my lender accept a private flood policy?
faqs.a: Federal rules require regulated lenders to accept private flood policies that meet set criteria. Ask your lender to confirm before you switch.
faqs.a_plain: Federal rules require regulated lenders to accept private flood policies that meet set criteria. Ask your lender to confirm before you switch.

faqs.q: What is an elevation certificate?
faqs.a: A FEMA form completed by a surveyor or engineer that records the building's elevation relative to expected flood levels. Many insurers use it to price flood.
faqs.a_plain: A FEMA form completed by a surveyor or engineer that records the building's elevation relative to expected flood levels. Many insurers use it to price flood.

faqs.q: Is there a waiting period?
faqs.a: Most flood policies have one before coverage begins, though some private policies differ. Check the specific policy, especially during hurricane season.
faqs.a_plain: Most flood policies have one before coverage begins, though some private policies differ. Check the specific policy, especially during hurricane season.

faqs.q: How much does private flood insurance cost in Florida?
faqs.a: What drives the price is the property itself: its location and flood zone, its age, roof and construction, its wind-mitigation features, the coverage limits and deductibles chosen, and its claims history.
faqs.a_plain: What drives the price is the property itself: its location and flood zone, its age, roof and construction, its wind-mitigation features, the coverage limits and deductibles chosen, and its claims history.

items.text: Flood zone
An elevation certificate (FEMA Form FF-206-FY-22-152) if one exists
items.why: it records the building's elevation and can change the premium considerably

items.text: Foundation type, height of the first floor above ground and any flood openings
Whether utilities such as the air handler and water heater are raised
The building and contents limits you want
Prior flood claims and any current flood policy, including whether coverage has been continuous
